message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"5.1","text":"So, on the following day in Tyre, I went to the quiet place as we had arranged. After seeing and greeting the others, together with some additional people, but not seeing Appion, I asked why he was not present. Someone said that he had been physically unwell since the previous evening. When I said that it was reasonable for us to set out immediately and visit him, almost everyone requested that I first hold a discussion with them and that then, in that way, I would be able to visit him as well. Once everyone had come to a single decision, I began to speak:","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"δυσαρρώστως αὐτὸν ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἑσπέρας ἐσχηκέναι τὸ σωμάτιον","chosen":"he had been physically unwell since the previous evening","rationale":"The idiom describes the poor condition of his body. The diminutive σωμάτιον need not imply literal smallness and is represented naturally by “physically.”"},{"source_quote":"πρότερον διαλεχθῆναί με αὐτοῖς","chosen":"that I first hold a discussion with them","rationale":"διαλέγομαι can mean converse, discourse, or debate; “hold a discussion” suits the requested address without predetermining its degree of formality."},{"source_quote":"εἶθ’ οὕτως κἀκεῖνον ἐπισκέψασθαι δύνασθαι αὐτόν","chosen":"and that then, in that way, I would be able to visit him as well","rationale":"The rendering takes κἀκεῖνον as the object of ἐπισκέψασθαι and αὐτόν as the accusative subject of δύνασθαι, referring to Clement from the participants’ perspective. English naturally returns that third-person reference to the narrator’s first person."},{"source_quote":"μιᾶς οὖν πάντων γνώμης γενομένης","chosen":"Once everyone had come to a single decision","rationale":"Literally, “when one opinion of all had come about”; the rendering expresses their resulting unanimity."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"κἀκεῖνον ἐπισκέψασθαι δύνασθαι αὐτόν","issue":"The main rendering analyzes κἀκεῖνον as the object of ἐπισκέψασθαι and αὐτόν as the accusative subject of δύνασθαι, contextually referring to Clement with a shift from the preceding first-person με to the participants’ third-person perspective. Alternatively, κἀκεῖνον and αὐτόν may be understood as an emphatic or resumptive double reference to Appion, yielding the sense “visit that man himself.” The construction is unusual but does not require deleting either accusative.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"5.2","text":"“Yesterday, when I left this place, friends, I admit that I could not get to sleep, because I was deeply preoccupied with the discussion that was going to take place with Appion. As I lay awake, the stratagems I had devised against him in Rome rushed into my mind. They were as follows. From childhood I, Clement, had loved truth, had sought the things that matter to the soul, and had spent my time on refutations and demonstrations; but because I could find nothing definitive, the mental strain drove me into illness. And indeed, while I lay ill, Appion arrived in Rome. He was a friend of my father and stayed as my guest. When he learned that I was bedridden, he came in to see me, since he was not unversed in medicine, and asked why I had taken to bed. I was well aware that the man held Jews in deep hatred—so much so that he had written many books against them—and that he had now taken Simon himself as a friend, not out of a love of learning, but because he knew him to be a Samaritan, a Jew-hater, and someone who had come forward against the Jews. For that reason he had drawn him close, so that he could learn from him something to use against the Jews—","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τῆς πρὸς Ἀππίωνα μελλούσης ἔσεσθαι ζητήσεως","chosen":"the discussion that was going to take place with Appion","rationale":"ζήτησις can denote an inquiry, dispute, or debate. “Discussion” leaves its precise character open while the wider narrative supplies its adversarial aspect."},{"source_quote":"τὰ ἐν Ῥώμῃ πρὸς αὐτόν μοι μεμηχανημένα","chosen":"the stratagems I had devised against him in Rome","rationale":"μηχανάομαι denotes contriving or devising, while πρὸς αὐτόν is contextually adversarial rather than merely relational."},{"source_quote":"εἰς ἀνασκευὰς καὶ κατασκευὰς","chosen":"on refutations and demonstrations","rationale":"The paired terms denote arguments that respectively dismantle and establish a position; alternatives include “disproofs and proofs” or “negative and positive arguments.”"},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ τῆς συνοίας ἐξώκειλα εἰς νόσον","chosen":"the mental strain drove me into illness","rationale":"σύνοια can denote intense thought, anxiety, or distress arising from reflection; “mental strain” preserves both the intellectual and harmful dimensions."},{"source_quote":"πατρικὸς ὢν μοι φίλος","chosen":"He was a friend of my father","rationale":"πατρικὸς φίλος can mean a paternal or inherited family friend. The immediate first-person construction most naturally indicates a friend connected with Clement’s father."},{"source_quote":"σαμαρέα αὐτὸν οἶδεν μισοϊουδαῖόν τε ὄντα","chosen":"he knew him to be a Samaritan, a Jew-hater","rationale":"The ethnic designation and the compound μισοϊουδαῖος are retained distinctly rather than treating Samaritan identity itself as equivalent to hatred of Jews."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἵνα δύνατο κατὰ Ἰουδαίων τι παρ’ αὐτοῦ μανθάνειν","issue":"The form δύνατο after ἵνα is morphosyntactically unusual by classical standards but can be understood as late or nonclassical use of a past indicative in a purpose clause. The proposed optative is only a possible normalization, not the supplied reading.","proposed_reading":"ἵνα δύναιτο κατὰ Ἰουδαίων τι παρ’ αὐτοῦ μανθάνειν","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"5.3","text":"Knowing these things beforehand about Appion, as soon as he asked the cause of my illness, I answered in pretense, “I suffer what young men suffer, and my soul aches.” He replied, “Child, trust me as you would a father and tell me: what is the illness of your soul?” Once again I sighed in pretense, as though ashamed to speak about being in love. By my silence and by looking downward, I gave him grounds to suspect what I wanted to suggest. Convinced that I was truly in love with a woman, he said, “There is nothing in life that cannot receive help. For when I myself was young, I fell in love with a most distinguished woman. Not only did I consider it impossible to obtain her; I did not even hope ever to address her. Nevertheless, I happened to meet an Egyptian who was highly accomplished in the practices of magicians. After he befriended me, I disclosed my passion, and he not only placed himself at my disposal for everything I wanted, but, endeavoring to be even more lavish toward me, did not begrudge teaching me also the incantation through which I obtained her. Persuaded by that secret instruction of his and by the unstinting generosity of the man who taught me, after I had succeeded once, I stopped being in love.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Τὰ νέων πάσχω","chosen":"I suffer what young men suffer","rationale":"The compact expression literally refers to “the things of young men.” The rendering preserves Appion’s intended inference of youthful erotic distress without adding it directly to Clement’s words."},{"source_quote":"διά γε τῆς σιωπῆς καὶ τοῦ κάτω νεύειν","chosen":"By my silence and by looking downward","rationale":"κάτω νεύειν can mean lowering or inclining the head; “looking downward” conveys the visible gesture of affected embarrassment."},{"source_quote":"ὁ δὲ ἐρᾶν με γυναικὸς ἀληθῶς ἀναπεισθεὶς ἔφη","chosen":"Convinced that I was truly in love with a woman, he said","rationale":"ἀληθῶς can qualify either ἐρᾶν (“truly in love”) or ἀναπεισθείς (“truly convinced”). The main rendering attaches it to the supposed love because Appion interprets Clement’s affected behavior as evidence of a real passion; the alternative is “Truly convinced that I was in love with a woman.”"},{"source_quote":"οὐ μόνον αὐτῆς τυχεῖν ἡγούμην ἀδύνατον εἶναι, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ προσαγορεῦσαί ποτε ἤλπιζον","chosen":"Not only did I consider it impossible to obtain her; I did not even hope ever to address her","rationale":"The coordinated clauses express an escalation from regarding possession of her as impossible to lacking even the hope of ever speaking to her."},{"source_quote":"πάνυ τὰ μάγων ἀκριβοῦντι","chosen":"highly accomplished in the practices of magicians","rationale":"ἀκριβόω here signifies exact mastery or thorough knowledge; τὰ μάγων denotes the matters or practices belonging to magicians."},{"source_quote":"καὶ φιλωθεὶς ἐκφαίνω μου τὸν ἔρωτα","chosen":"After he befriended me, I disclosed my passion","rationale":"The passive φιλωθείς can mean being loved or treated as a friend. “Befriended” fits the ensuing disclosure, while ἐκφαίνω is represented according to the sense of its vivid historical present."},{"source_quote":"τὴν ἐπαοιδήν, δι’ ἧς ἔτυχον","chosen":"the incantation through which I obtained her","rationale":"ἐπαοιδή is a sung spell or incantation. Although the object of ἔτυχον is implicit here, the earlier αὐτῆς τυχεῖν supplies the woman as its contextual object; an alternative is “through which I succeeded.”"},{"source_quote":"ἐκ δὲ τῆς ἐκείνου λαθραίας ὑποδείξεως πεισθεὶς τῇ τοῦ διδάξαντος ἀφθονίᾳ","chosen":"Persuaded by that secret instruction of his and by the unstinting generosity of the man who taught me","rationale":"The dative τῇ … ἀφθονίᾳ is taken instrumentally alongside ἐκ τῆς … ὑποδείξεως. An alternative is “persuaded by that secret instruction of his to trust in the teacher’s unstinting generosity.”"},{"source_quote":"καὶ ἅπαξ ἐπιτυχών, ἐπαυσάμην τοῦ ἔρωτος","chosen":"after I had succeeded once, I stopped being in love","rationale":"Placing “once” after “succeeded” explicitly preserves the numerical force of ἅπαξ rather than reducing it to a temporal conjunction meaning merely “after.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"δαψιλέστερον πρὸς μὲ φιλοτιμούμενος","issue":"The confirmed print has μὲ with a grave accent. The context provisionally supports understanding it as the pronoun με, “me,” rather than as an incomplete μέν; the proposed reading regularizes the accent but is not the supplied text.","proposed_reading":"δαψιλέστερον πρὸς με φιλοτιμούμενος","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"5.4","text":"“Therefore, if you too have suffered something of this kind, as humans do, put your confidence in us and set your mind at ease, for within seven days I will make you obtain her without fail.” When I heard this, I kept my own purpose in view and said, “Forgive me for not fully believing that magic is real, for I have already had experience of many people making many promises and then failing to fulfill them. Still, your promise presses me and leads me to hope. Yet I am afraid when I consider whether demons may sometimes fail to obey magicians in the things they are commanded to do.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εἰ καὶ σὺ τοιοῦτόν τι πέπονθας ἀνθρωπίνως","chosen":"if you too have suffered something of this kind, as humans do","rationale":"ἀνθρωπίνως marks the experience as human or natural to humanity, not as morally commendable."},{"source_quote":"θάρσησον ἡμῖν πρὸς τὸ ἀμέριμνον","chosen":"put your confidence in us and set your mind at ease","rationale":"The text has the plural ἡμῖν, “in us,” although Appion is speaking. It may be an inclusive or self-referential plural; the translation preserves it rather than silently changing it to “me.” πρὸς τὸ ἀμέριμνον expresses the intended freedom from worry."},{"source_quote":"μαγείαν ὑφεστάναι","chosen":"that magic is real","rationale":"ὑφίστημι in this construction concerns actual existence or reality, not merely the practice of magic."},{"source_quote":"πολλῶν γὰρ πολλὰ ἐπαγγελλομένων καὶ διαψευσαμένων ἤδη πεπείραμαι","chosen":"I have already had experience of many people making many promises and then failing to fulfill them","rationale":"διαψεύδομαι can denote proving false, disappointing expectations, or failing in a claim. “Failing to fulfill them” makes the relation to the promises explicit without alleging a particular motive."},{"source_quote":"δυσωπεῖ με καὶ εἰς ἐλπίδας ἄγει ἡ σὴ ὑπόσχεσις","chosen":"your promise presses me and leads me to hope","rationale":"δυσωπέω may mean shame, constrain, move, or win someone over. “Presses me” retains Clement’s affected reluctance without implying that he already believes Appion."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"5.5","text":"Appion said, “Concede that I know more about these matters than you do. Yet, so that you may not think you have heard nothing from me in answer to what you said, learn how it is that demons are compelled to submit to magicians in the matters about which they receive commands. Just as it is impossible for a soldier to contradict his commander, and the commanders themselves cannot disobey a king—for if anyone contradicts those set over him, he is certainly judged deserving of punishment—so it is impossible for demons not to serve their angelic commanders. When adjured by appeal to those angels, they shudder and yield, knowing well that if they disobey, they will certainly be punished. But even the angels themselves, when magicians adjure them by the one who is superior, obey, for fear that they may be judged guilty of disobedience and perish. For if all beings that possess life and reason did not foresee the punishment coming from the superior one, confusion would have arisen, with all of them rebelling against one another.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Ταῦτα ἐμοὶ σοῦ μᾶλλον συγχώρει εἰδέναι","chosen":"Concede that I know more about these matters than you do","rationale":"συγχωρέω here asks Clement to concede or grant Appion’s asserted superior knowledge, not to give Appion permission to acquire knowledge."},{"source_quote":"πῶς ἀνάγκην ἔχουσιν οἱ δαίμονες τοῖς μάγοις ὑπείκειν","chosen":"how it is that demons are compelled to submit to magicians","rationale":"Literally, the demons “have necessity” to yield. “Are compelled” expresses the asserted necessity without introducing a distinct external agent."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς αὐτῶν ἡγουμένοις ἀγγέλοις","chosen":"their angelic commanders","rationale":"The participial noun ἡγουμένοις identifies angels who lead or command the demons; the phrase need not imply that the demons possess the angels."},{"source_quote":"καθ’ ὧν ὁρκιζόμενοι φρίττοντες· εἴκουσιν","chosen":"When adjured by appeal to those angels, they shudder and yield","rationale":"In adjuration language, κατά with the genitive identifies the authority invoked. The participle φρίττοντες is rendered together with εἴκουσιν despite the printed high stop. An alternative is “being adjured by them, they yield with trembling.”"},{"source_quote":"κατὰ τοῦ κρείττονος ὑπὸ μάγων ὁρκιζόμενοι","chosen":"when magicians adjure them by the one who is superior","rationale":"κρείττων is comparative and may mean the greater, stronger, or higher-ranking one. “The one who is superior” preserves the hierarchy without identifying the referent beyond what the passage states."},{"source_quote":"τὴν ἐκ τοῦ κρείττονος δίκην","chosen":"the punishment coming from the superior one","rationale":"δίκη can denote justice, judgment, or penalty. The repeated warnings of punishment and destruction favor “punishment” here, while κρείττων is rendered consistently with the preceding clause."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"καθ’ ὧν ὁρκιζόμενοι φρίττοντες· εἴκουσιν","issue":"The confirmed edition prints a high stop after φρίττοντες. The translation provisionally reads the participle with εἴκουσιν as a continuous construction, while preserving the marked editorial break in this disclosure; no replacement wording is required for a defensible translation.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
